extracted.intended_audience: Federal agency NEPA practitioners, agency counsel, Tribal/state/local governments, and other stakeholders involved in NEPA implementation
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and final-rule explanations for CEQ's revisions to the NEPA regulations, intended to guide Federal agencies on definitions, documentation, public engagement, and procedural requirements for EAs, EISs, categorical exclusions, and related NEPA practices. Focuses on what agencies must or should do to comply with the updated regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency NEPA program transparency via websites/IT tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must provide on their websites or through other information technology tools their agency NEPA procedures and a list of EAs and EISs that are in development and complete; CEQ proposed to change “other means” to “other information technology tools” and remove “environmental” before “documents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement is intended to promote transparency and help the public identify active NEPA reviews; it does not require agencies to publish the documents themselves, only a list of documents in development or completed. Agencies may cross-reference other repositories (Federal Register, EPA's EIS database) to reduce duplication. Agencies have discretion to determine when a NEPA review is sufficiently in development to list it, and the provision does not require posting pre-decisional or non-public information. CEQ encourages (but does not require) including additional items listed in paragraphs (a)(1)-(a)(4) and encourages posting environmental documents; interagency coordination of websites and shared databases is promoted but not limited to listed technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant — definition and consistent terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ adds definition of “applicant” as a non-Federal entity that seeks an action by a Federal agency and clarifies that this term is inclusive of project sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ will use the term 'applicant' consistently throughout the regulations, replacing references to 'non-Federal entity' and 'project sponsor' for clarity. Agencies should adopt consistent language in their NEPA procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical exclusion (CE) definition and extraordinary circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical exclusions are categories of actions that an agency has determined 'normally does not significantly affect the quality of the human environment'; CEQ retained the word 'normally' and explained it to mean 'in the absence of extraordinary circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing a CE, an agency must provide for consideration of extraordinary circumstances to identify when a specific action that falls within the category is not of the normal variety and therefore requires further analysis (documentation under §1501.4(b)(1) or an EA/EIS). CEs are not exemptions from NEPA's requirement to prepare an EIS for a major Federal action that significantly affects the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communities with environmental justice concerns — definition and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ defines 'communities with environmental justice concerns' to mean communities 'that may not experience environmental justice as defined . . . in §1508.1(m),' and indicates agencies may use available screening tools (examples: Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool and EJScreen Tool).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have flexibility to develop procedures for identifying such communities in their agency NEPA procedures and are encouraged to make use of available tools and resources. The definition is not intended to make communities self-identify; agencies are incumbent on proactively identifying such communities. CEQ may provide additional guidance in future as tools/methods develop; CEQ also encourages robust public engagement with EJ stakeholders and anticipates agencies will develop more expertise over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperating agency — statutory consistency and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ finalizes the definition of 'cooperating agency' consistent with NEPA section 107(a)(3)/111(2): a lead agency may designate as a cooperating agency 'any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency that has jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to any environmental impact involved in a proposal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declines to expand the definition to include agencies merely 'involved in a proposal' as overly broad. CEQ encourages agencies to invite local governments and Tribes to participate as cooperating agencies where they have special expertise. The definition does not include non-governmental organizations or quasi-governmental organizations as cooperating agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects or Impacts — scope and examples (direct, indirect, cumulative, EJ, climate, Tribal resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ restores and clarifies the definition of 'effects' to include direct, indirect, and cumulative effects and adds explicit examples: 'disproportionate and adverse effects on communities with environmental justice concerns, whether direct, indirect, or cumulative' and 'climate change-related effects' (including both contributions to climate change and effects of climate change on the action). CEQ also adds 'effects on Tribal resources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects must be reasonably foreseeable; direct, indirect, and cumulative are categories of reasonably foreseeable effects. The list of examples is non-exhaustive. CEQ declines to narrow cumulative effects analysis only to 'significant' cumulative effects in the regulatory text, and declines to adopt overly specific additional examples requested by commenters. Qualitative analysis can be sufficient in some cases (CEQ notes guidance exists on cumulative effects). CEQ rejects attempts to remove 'cumulative' from the definition or to restore 'reasonably close causal relationship' language removed earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Assessment (EA) — definition and agency responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ revises the definition of 'environmental assessment' to 'for which a Federal agency is responsible' (rather than 'prepared by a Federal agency') and clarifies that an EA is prepared when a proposed action is not likely to have a significant effect or the significance is unknown and is used to support an agency's determination whether to prepare an EIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant or agency-directed contractor may prepare an EA, but the agency is responsible for the accuracy of its contents. The definition cross-references to part 1502 and §1501.6 (FONSIs). CEQ declines to add further text on mitigated FONSIs in the definition because §1501.6 already addresses mitigated FONSIs, but the EA definition continues to support that determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental document — inclusion of documented CE determinations and RODs
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ changes the 'environmental document' definition to add 'record of decision' and a 'documented categorical exclusion determination' to reflect agency practice of documenting some CE determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented CE determinations are part of the environmental document definition; undocumented CEs are excluded. CEQ considered but declined to narrow this definition; agencies should consider this broader regulatory definition when applying other provisions that reference 'environmental document.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) — definitional consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ makes a minor edit in the definition of 'environmental impact statement' changing 'as required' to 'that is required' for consistency with section 111(6) of NEPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a non-substantive edit to align regulatory language with statutory text; agencies should treat the EIS definition consistent with section 111(6) of NEPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Justice — definition and use of 'cumulative impacts'
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ adds a definition of 'environmental justice' as 'the just treatment and meaningful involvement of all people so that they are fully protected from disproportionate and adverse human health and environmental effects and hazards, and have equitable access to a healthy, sustainable, and resilient environment,' and uses the phrase 'cumulative impacts' (rather than 'cumulative effects') in the EJ context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declines to define 'cumulative impacts' at this time, citing evolving science; it will consider guidance later. The definition is consistent with longstanding agency practice of evaluating potential effects to communities experiencing disproportionate and adverse impacts and ensuring meaningful engagement. CEQ will consider whether additional guidance is required to help agencies apply EJ consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmentally preferable alternative — definition and selection among analyzed alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ adds a definition of 'environmentally preferable alternative' as the alternative or alternatives that will best promote the national environmental policy in section 101 of NEPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies identify the environmentally preferable alternative among alternatives analyzed in the EIS (the proposed action, no action, and reasonable alternatives). The definition does not require agencies to consider alternatives beyond those analyzed, and agencies are not required to adopt the environmentally preferable alternative as their final decision. CEQ declines to add language that the environmentally preferable alternative must be 'reasonable' since the alternatives analyzed in an EIS already meet the 'reasonable alternatives' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of scoping with EA process — agency discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ removed a paragraph urging combining an agency's EA process with its scoping process but clarified in §1501.5(k) that agencies can employ scoping at their discretion when it will improve the efficiency and effectiveness of EAs, including combining scoping with a comment period on a draft EA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ acknowledges that integrating scoping with EA can be inclusive and efficient; agencies may adopt such practices where appropriate. CEQ removed redundant regulatory text but left explicit discretion and authority for agencies to use scoping when beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classified proposals — limiting withheld information and releasing unclassified portions
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ declines to modify paragraph addressing classified proposals; the longstanding provision encourages agencies to withhold only what is necessary for protection of classified information and to structure the document so that unclassified portions can be made available for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies handling classified information should withhold only necessary classified content and organize documents to enable release of unclassified material for public participation, consistent with existing regulations dating to 1978.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency actions — special arrangements for EAs
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision regarding emergency actions is similar to CEQ's emergency process for EISs but relates to activities that would not require preparation of an EIS; some agencies may have programs focused on emergency actions and may need special arrangements for their EAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special arrangements for emergency EAs could address document format, special distribution and public involvement procedures, and timing considerations. Agencies with established emergency procedures may rely on those processes to ensure efficient NEPA compliance in emergencies.
